P01.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. In one season she called a play the finest of the year in March and, after seeing it again, tedious in April. The stage manager's logs show that the cast, the staging, and even the running time were unchanged between her two visits, and a later scholar found her reviews in other seasons reversing themselves about as often. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: In 2015 a city passed an ordinance limiting where street vendors could park their carts. The city's inspectors worked through a list of every licensed cart, block by block, checking each one once a month, and a vendor found in a restricted zone received a written warning and, on a second offense, a fine. In the first year's records, single-cart owners and the city's largest fleet of food trucks show the same number of checks per cart and the same share of warnings that became fines. Asked about its first year, most of the vendors interviewed for one study described the city's enforcement of the ordinance as ______.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: In the spring of 1974 a river broke through its levees and flooded some four hundred homes in a farming district. Engineers at the ministry knew that a drainage canal it had dug the year before had weakened the levee at the very point where it broke. Rather than admit this, the ministry paid each family through a church charity that did not name its source, and reporters learned where the money had come from only twelve years later. In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: For most of the eighteenth century, two towns on opposite banks of a salmon river tore down each other's fish weirs whenever the run was good. In 1790 a canal company petitioned to buy the fishing rights of both banks, and the two councils signed a truce and hired one lawyer between them to fight the petition. While the case dragged on, the magistrates' books record almost no cut weirs. The company withdrew its petition in 1815, and within a season each town was cutting the other's weirs again. Writing a century later, one historian called the truce between the towns from 1790 to 1815 ______.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: In the 1920s an amateur naturalist began studying the bluebirds that nested in forty wooden boxes along the fences of her family's farm. Each morning at seven she walked the fence line from the barn to the creek, stopping at every box. Her notebooks from six springs survive with no day missing, and every page uses the same four columns: eggs, chicks, food brought, and weather. Biologists decades later could therefore compare any two boxes, or any two springs, entry for entry. In a review of early bird studies, one biologist called the naturalist's approach ______.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version the ship's name and its sailing terms have become sounds without meaning: the topsail is now "the top of the hill," and the home port a name found on no map. Several verses no longer make sense, and the singers who sang them could not say what they meant. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: For most of the 1960s a retired surgeon sat on the nine-member board of trustees of a county hospital. The board's rules allowed only its finance committee to place a spending request on the agenda, and she chaired that committee for the whole decade. Department heads seeking a new ward or a costly machine sent their requests to the committee, which met in her office; of the forty or so requests that arrived each year, about five reached the full board, and the trustees approved nearly every one they saw. In an oral history recorded decades later, one fellow trustee called her the board's ______ during those years.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: In 1948 a new regional health board took charge of every hospital in a rural county, among them the old stone county hospital. The board's own records showed that patients there died after surgery less often than anywhere else in the county. Over the next ten years the board built three new hospitals in other towns from the stone building's floor plan, staffed each with its number of nurses per ward, and gave each its rules for washing and for visiting, while the county hospital went on as before. Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. She would not travel and distrusted the mail. Every spring he rode out to the farm, took the year's poems back to her printer in a sealed packet he never opened, and returned in the summer with the printed proofs, which she corrected alone. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had long sold their grain. Over the next decade it bought the harvest of nearly every farm in the district at the town's scales and leased both of the town's warehouses. By the late 1790s the millers downriver could buy grain from no one else, and each autumn they paid whatever price the house named. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: When a novelist died in 1931, she left the manuscript of her last novel, a story of dockworkers' families set in the 1880s, to her longtime editor. The editor wrote to her family that it was the best book she had written, and over the next twenty years told everyone who asked about it that it needed more time. The editor's press printed four other dockside novels in those years. The manuscript turned up in a desk drawer after the editor's death, without a single pencil mark, and was printed in 1953. In a study published decades later, one scholar argued that this editor had ______ the book.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: In 1952 a state marketing board began buying the reed baskets that households on a small fishing island had woven for generations. By then only a handful of elderly islanders still wove, since the fishing crews had gone over to cheap tin pails in the 1930s. The board paid a fixed price for every basket and shipped them to mainland fish markets. Through the 1950s younger islanders sat with those elders to learn the stitches, and by 1975 most households again kept a basket on the frame through the winter evenings. Visiting the island in 1975, one folklorist concluded that the board's purchases had ______ the craft.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: In 1907 a composer built one movement of his first symphony on a folk tune he had heard in a fishing village. In the village it was a slow lament, sung at funerals with each note held long. The composer kept every note and gave the tune to the full orchestra at twice the speed, over a quick, skipping rhythm in the drums, so that audiences at the premiere tapped their feet to it. Comparing the symphony with the village version, one critic observed that the composer had ______ the tune.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait, a place with thin soil and almost no trade of its own. The strait's merchants soon moved their route to a deeper channel thirty miles south, and for decades only the garrison's supply ship called. The empire still spent more each year on the island's garrison than on any province, its keys were carried in procession on the anniversary of its capture, and a painting of its harbor hung behind the throne. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: From 1884 to 1910 a mining valley's only newspaper was a four-page weekly sold at the pithead for a penny. A miner who believed a foreman had cheated him on the weight of his coal could bring the matter to the paper, whose editor heard the miner and the foreman together and printed in the next issue a short finding that went against the miner about as often as for him. By the 1890s both the miners and the company usually accepted the paper's finding as final, and the valley's courts heard almost none of these disputes. Writing a century later, one historian called the weekly the miners' ______.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. Swollen by snowmelt, the river left its winding bed for a straight course down the valley floor, and the fast water cut into the soft soil wherever it ran. When it fell back, it left a ravine some twenty feet deep along the valley's full length, with the old riverbed lying dry beside it. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: In 1958 a retired wheat farmer published a memoir of his forty years on the plains, with a chapter for each season of the farm year. The chapter on planting winter wheat spends two pages on the wheat and then moves on to his grandfather's violin, the history of the county road, and a recipe for plum jam, returning to the wheat in its final paragraph. Nearly every chapter follows that pattern, so a reader can lose track of which season the book has reached. Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: From 1951 to 1966 a chemist at a small university laboratory worked with a single technician, a young woman hired straight out of high school. The chemist disliked travel, never once attended a meeting, and answered letters from other scientists only through her. Each spring she spent a month visiting laboratories across the country, where she presented the year's results, took other chemists' questions, and settled the exchanges of samples on which his later papers depended. One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: In 1974 a state commission published a report on the last dam on the river, which had stood for sixty years. For a decade a small anglers' club had argued for removal against the power company at county meetings, while the state's papers seldom printed its letters and legislators declined to hear its speakers. The commission, chaired by a retired judge, found removal both affordable and lawful. Over the following years the state's largest papers and several legislators came to treat removal as one serious option among others. In her history of the river, one journalist wrote that the report had ______ the debate over the dam.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: From 1878 to 1901 a single inspector examined the cargo landed at a small river port for the customs service. He took each captain's word for what the crates held, and smugglers soon learned to mark crates of brandy as machine parts and crates of tobacco as books. His reports record almost no seizures in twenty-three years, and two captains later wrote in their memoirs of how easily his port could be worked. Reading his reports a century later, one historian described the inspector as ______.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. After a naval raid on the port in 1914, the army built barracks beside the town's station to house troops who could reach the city's docks by train within an hour. Through the 1920s three regiments took turns living there, drilling on the old fairground, and the town's shops lived largely on the soldiers' pay. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: In 1790 a country surveyor published a map of the kingdom that went through eleven printings in twenty years. Rival maps were engraved on sheets a yard wide, meant to hang in a study or lie open on a library table. The surveyor printed his on linen in sixteen panels hinged to fold flat, and the copies that survive, most of them owned by cattle drovers and traveling merchants, are worn through along the folds. Comparing it with other maps of its day, one historian describes the surveyor's map as, above all, ______.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: A weavers' guild built a stone hall beside the market square of a river town in 1580, and the guild was dissolved in 1760. The council repainted its carved front after every hard winter and hung it with lamps on feast days. Its doors stayed locked, and the council minutes record no meeting, sale or service held in or at the hall in those hundred years. In the century after 1760, one historian writes, the hall served chiefly as the town's ______.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The outbreak was a beetle whose larvae bore through the heartwood of living oaks, feeding there for several years before they emerge. The trees went on leafing out and growing as before, and cores drilled from a dozen trunks in 2016 came up in crumbs and short pieces, broken at every point where a larva's tunnel had crossed them. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: In 1871 the hand-loom weavers of a hill district pooled their dues to buy a stone hall in the market town. Over the following decades the mill owners bought up the market, the bank, and most council seats, and turned the rules of each against home weaving. The hall's deed, held by the weavers jointly, was the one title in town they could not acquire, and inside its walls the old price agreement and the apprentice rules still held. The weavers refused every offer for it, the last in 1919. For the next half century, one historian has argued, the hall served the district's weavers chiefly as their ______.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: In 1968 a city opened a new central library, designed by a young architect, on the site of an old train station. The old library had stood at the top of forty steps on a hill, and readers there had filled out slips for clerks to fetch books from closed stacks. The new one stood beside the main bus terminal with ramps at every door and a ground floor level with the street, and its shelves stood open to anyone who walked in. Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: In 1928 a record company made the first recording of an old ballad from the hill counties, about a ferryman drowned in a flood. In the hill counties it had been sung only in church at funerals, and its last verse was a prayer for the ferryman's soul. The record kept the hill singers' hard voices and fiddle, replaced the prayer with a verse naming the river and the year of the flood, and was sold to the dance halls, where it was played between reels. One folklorist has argued that the 1928 recording had ______ the ballad.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: For six centuries a small monastery stood at the top of the only pass between two mountain valleys, each ruled by its own lord. Each lord's soldiers held his own end of the road, and neither lord trusted the other's toll keepers. Every cart that came up the pass stopped at the monastery gate, where the monks listed its load and sealed it with the abbot's stamp, refusing the seal to any cart carrying weapons. Toll keepers in both valleys waved sealed carts through and searched any other to the last sack. In a history of the pass, one scholar described the monastery as, above all, the region's ______.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: In 1922 two neighboring states signed a treaty dividing the water of a river that crossed both, and much of its later history turned on its seventh clause. That clause set the method for measuring the river's yearly flow, and every other clause stated each state's share as a fraction of the flow so measured. When a court struck the method down in 1961 because the gauge it named had been removed, none of the other clauses could be applied, and the two states had to negotiate a new treaty from the beginning. Writing in 1980, one legal historian called the seventh clause the treaty's ______.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: In 1882 a forty-page pamphlet on the rights of tenant farmers appeared in one rural province, the same year a tenants' movement formed there. Its chapters set out, step by step, how to call a meeting, word a petition to a landlord, and file a complaint with the county court. Branches of the movement kept copies on the table at every meeting, and members wrote corrections into the margins wherever a court's procedure had changed, mailing them to the printer for the next edition. Looking back, one historian called the pamphlet the movement's ______ in its first decade.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: From 1820 to 1860 a mountain village was governed by a council of four elected members, who appointed a secretary to keep the minutes of their meetings. The secretary also kept the council's accounts, and each spring read aloud to the village assembly every payment the council had made without a vote of the members. After two such readings, members repaid sums they had taken for fencing their own fields. In 1841 the members moved to end the yearly reading, and the assembly refused to let them. In the village's records, one historian has argued, the secretary appears above all as the council's ______.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. From its first keel, the yard wrote down each hull's timber, builder, and buyer, and added every later repair, sale, and wreck. When two families quarreled over a boat, or a buyer wanted to know what a secondhand hull had been through, they walked to the yard to look it up. By 1921 its books held the life of nearly every boat on that coast. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: In 1868 the twenty-four football clubs of a northern county's league, from its towns and villages alike, adopted a new rule for their matches. Before it, a scrum could hold forty players kicking at one another's shins. The rule ended a scrum as soon as the ball was held and barred any kick that missed the ball. The county papers, which had listed dozens of broken legs a season, listed four in 1870. Scores and crowds stayed much as they had been, and the scrum, now brief, remained the heart of every match. Looking back, one sports historian argued that the rule of 1868 had ______ the game.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: For centuries the villages of one mountain valley marked the end of the olive harvest with a night procession, led by singers, from the church to the presses. After a road reached the valley in the 1950s, buses brought visitors each November, and the villages moved the procession from midnight to early evening so that visitors could watch. Singers began wearing costumes copied from old photographs, a narrator explained each verse over loudspeakers to folding chairs along the route, and the families who had always led it now rehearsed for weeks. Writing in 1990, one folklorist concluded that the changes of the previous fifty years had ______ the custom.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: In 1712 a market town ordered every household to send one adult each spring to spend two days clearing the town's drainage ditches, or else to pay a fine of one shilling. Over the next century the council excused, one group at a time, members of the militia, shopkeepers on market days, anyone who kept a horse for hire, and anyone past fifty. By the 1890s fewer than one household in five still owed the duty, and the clerk's books show the ditches only partly cleared in most springs. By 1900, one historian observes, the ditch rule had become ______.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: A state forestry service founded in 1911 managed the timber of a mountainous province, and one of its fourteen districts was a narrow valley in the eastern hills. The service had money to survey only one district, and in 1912 its foresters counted and measured every tree on the valley's slopes. For the next thirty years it set the yearly cutting limit for all fourteen districts by multiplying the valley's figures by each district's area, on the assumption that the other slopes grew timber at the same rate. One historian argues that, from 1911 to 1940, the valley was above all the service's ______.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: In 1880 a geologist proposed that the hot springs of a mountain basin were fed by rain falling on a ridge to the north. The proposal covered all twelve of the basin's springs, and geologists generally accepted it. The 1931 survey poured dye into fissures along the ridge and found it, weeks later, in four of the springs and in none of the other eight, and textbooks of the following decade name the ridge as the source of those four alone. One historian of geology writes that the 1931 survey ______ the ridge hypothesis.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. The novel is told entirely through his letters to a brother overseas, so readers meet the sisters only as he describes them. Critics have noted that the elder sister, whom the letters treat warmly, comes across as generous, while the younger, whom he distrusts, seems grasping in scenes where the two behave almost identically. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: Above a harbor town, a river crosses six miles of reedy marsh, and below the marsh the lower river runs past the town's quays to the bay. Each spring herring that have come up the river lay their eggs in the marsh's warm, shallow pools, where reeds hide the young from larger fish. The young stay until autumn and then swim down into the lower river. Netting surveys below the marsh find that nearly every young herring caught past the quays hatched in those pools, and the river above the marsh holds almost none. One hydrologist has concluded that the marsh serves the lower river as a kind of ______.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: From 1880 to 1930 the weekly paper of a small river city carried an unsigned column on its front page. Three times in those years the provincial government proposed merging the city into the larger town across the river, and each time the column printed weekly attacks on the plan along with the names of residents who had signed petitions against it, and diaries from the period show whole families signing together. Each proposal was withdrawn within a year, and the city kept its own council until 1931. One historian of the city calls the column, over the fifty years it ran, the city's ______.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
